Accept additional cookies Reject additional cookies View cookies Hide cookie message Skip to main content News story Military Engineering Showcase highlights UK defence innovation Over 60 UK companies joined partners from over 20 nations to showcase military engineering solutions, strengthen collaboration and support UK defence exports. From: Ministry of Defence Published: 19 October 2026 Attendees at the Military Engineering Showcase The NAD Group brought together a range of SMEs and Primes to showcase UK military engineering capabilities to international partners and UK Defence stakeholders. 66 UK defence companies demonstrated solutions across domains from combat engineering to demining and force protection. International delegations from more than 20 nations attended to discuss common military engineering challenges and opportunities for collaboration. The event supported UK defence exports, strengthened international partnerships and showcased innovation from the UK’s industrial base. Hosted by National Armaments International (NA-Intl), the Military Engineering Showcase 2026 provided a forum for the UK Ministry of Defence, international partners and industry to share expertise, discuss common requirements and examine innovative technologies across the military engineering sector. Taking place on 5 and 6 October 2026, the event highlighted the UK’s military engineering capabilities across combat engineering, infrastructure, counter-explosive ordnance, demining, force protection, survivability and deployable infrastructure. Against a backdrop of increasing global instability and evolving security challenges, military engineering continues to play a vital role in supporting operational effectiveness, force protection, post-conflict recovery, and humanitarian assistance. The showcase is designed to strengthen collaboration between the British military, overseas partners and the UK’s innovative defence industry, much of which is made up of small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). These companies play a critical role in developing and manufacturing specialist capabilities for Defence, while export opportunities help sustain the expertise and resilience of the UK’s industrial base. Lieutenant Colonel Andrew Teeton MBE RE, Military Advisor Counter-Explosive Ordnance and CBRN, National Armaments - International, said: The UK military engineering sector is home to world-leading companies, many of them SMEs, that are passionate about supporting Defence. Through collaboration and export opportunities, we can help sustain the skills, expertise, and innovation needed to meet current and future military engineering requirements. Events like the Military Engineering demo help us enhance capability, improve interoperability and support a resilient UK industrial base by strengthening partnerships and sharing approaches to common challenges. The event featured presentations from UK military engineering specialists, networking opportunities with international delegations, capability demonstrations and industry briefings. Delegates had the opportunity to engage directly with the Export Support Team (EST), part of NA-International. Comprised of British Army officers and soldiers, the EST provides specialist military services and advice to UK defence and security companies and were on hand throughout the demonstration to share their expertise on current and emerging military engineering requirements. The Military Engineering Showcase supported wider efforts to strengthen international partnerships, promote UK defence collaboration and exports, and ensure military engineering capabilities continue to evolve in response to operational demands around the world. live_web_research.page_text: Uber begins self-driving robotaxi trial in Manchester | Uber | The Guardian Skip to main content Skip to navigation A self-driving Uber taxi launched with its partners Pony and Verne in the Croatian capital, Zagreb. Photograph: Uber View image in fullscreen A self-driving Uber taxi launched with its partners Pony and Verne in the Croatian capital, Zagreb. Photograph: Uber Uber Uber begins self-driving robotaxi trial in Manchester Company hails first step in rolling out technology across UK as first autonomous vehicles take to city’s streets Gwyn Topham Transport correspondent Wed 14 Oct 2026 14.11 BST Last modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 17.30 BST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Uber has begun a trial of autonomous vehicles on the streets of Manchester as it looks to bring robotaxis to cities around the UK. The first self-driving cars are operating, using the technology of its partner firms Pony and Verne, with whom Uber recently launched Europe’s first autonomous taxi service in the Croatian capital, Zagreb. Uber said it was “excited to take this first step toward making this technology accessible to people across the UK”. In social media posts, Verne said it had “started our autonomous vehicle testing in Manchester”, while Pony said there were “plans to bring robotaxis to the city” and that testing was under way. The tests involve the company mapping the streets of the city in north-west England with a safety driver behind the wheel and no passengers. Limited passenger services started last month in London , but with a safety driver in the front seat of cars supplied by Wayve under Transport for London’s licensing rules for private hire vehicles. The next steps are unclear. Opposition from Uber drivers, their unions and the capital’s politicians to the rollout of robotaxis is mounting. The GMB and ADCU unions have both said thousands of drivers jobs will be lost and have called for help for those affected. A critical report from London assembly’s transport committee this week called for the government to devolve authority over autonomous taxi services. It said there was “considerable uncertainty about many of the claimed benefits of autonomous passenger vehicles”, and fears over the impact on public transport and congestion, as well as safeguarding and accessibility for disabled passengers. There has been no official application to launch passenger services in Manchester so far. A spokesperson for Transport for Greater Manchester said it wanted the city’s taxis to be the safest in the country. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Business Today Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion “New technologies play an increasingly important role in the growth of our city region,” they said. “But they need to be introduced responsibly, safely and with real thought about what it means for our residents. “Although no applications have been made to operate driverless taxis in the Greater Manchester, we’re aware of potential interest from companies to do so. “Safety will always be our top priority, and we will need strong assurances that no vehicles will operate on our roads that pose any risk to residents.” Uber said it expected to offering robotaxi trips in as many as 15 cities worldwide by the end of 2026, mainly in the US and the Middle East. selected_records.title: Military Engineering Showcase highlights UK defence innovation

article.body:
UK military engineering showcase offers no evidence of autonomous-vehicle deployment

The Ministry of Defence says 66 UK defence companies demonstrated engineering solutions at the Military Engineering Showcase on 5–6 October, with delegations from more than 20 nations. Hosted by National Armaments International, the event covered areas including combat engineering, demining and force protection, and aimed to support defence exports and international collaboration.

The published account identifies no autonomous vehicle, autonomy stack, operating domain or vehicle-specific safety data. It also cites no AV permit, operating approval or passenger service. The showcase is evidence of an industry event, not an autonomous-vehicle deployment.
